ideas.title: Absorption-Ratio Throttle on an Inverse-Volatility Book
ideas.sketch: Each close, compute the 10x10 correlation matrix of daily log returns over the last 60 days and its top eigenvalue share AR60 = lambda_1/10 (the absorption ratio: fraction of cross-asset variance carried by one common factor). Also compute AR20 and the standardised shift dAR = (AR20 - mean(AR250)) / std(AR250). Base weights are inverse-60-day-volatility (risk-parity baseline), scaled so ex-ante portfolio vol is 7%, capped at 100% invested with the rest in cash. The stress throttle is s = 1 - smoothstep(dAR, 0.5, 2.5) mapped to [0.25, 1], so exposure is a smooth function of the stress state (no binary switch) and never below 25% of the vol-targeted book; target weights = s * base. Execution: every trading day move current weights toward target by lambda = 1/5 of the gap, then rescale the step so one-way turnover (half the sum of absolute changes) is at most 3.9% that day, which gives at most 19.5% in a 5-day week by construction; with a continuous target the step is nonzero every day, so trades occur on at least 3 days in every week. Drawdown argument: AR rose sharply into Sep-Oct 2008 and Feb-Mar 2020, and climbed slowly through 2022 as stock-bond correlation turned positive, so the throttle cuts exposure as correlations converge, i.e. exactly when diversification stops working; residual worst case is the loss taken while the throttle ramps (about 10 days to halve exposure under the 3.9% cap), estimated at 8-12% on a 7%-vol book in 2020, with 2022 the binding case because the state rises slowly. Net growth is an honest risk-parity return (roughly 4-5% real to 5-6% nominal after low ETF costs), with the improvement coming from avoiding correlated-drawdown states rather than from forecasting returns.

ideas.title: Stress-Mixture Covariance Sizing with Rank-1 Stress Prior
ideas.sketch: The stress state is not a throttle on the outputs but an input to the covariance used for sizing. Let p_t = clip((AR60_t - q50) / (q95 - q50), 0, 1), where q50 and q95 are the expanding-window 50th and 95th percentiles of AR60 (at least 2 years of history, no look-ahead). Build Sigma_t = (1 - p_t) * Sigma_sample(120d, Ledoit-Wolf shrunk) + p_t * Sigma_stress, where Sigma_stress = D (rho 11' + (1 - rho) I) D with D the 20-day vol diagonal and rho = 0.8: the single-factor 'everything sells off together' scenario, positive stock-bond correlation included, which is the 2008/2020/2022 failure mode. Weights come from equal-risk-contribution under Sigma_t (Newton or cyclical coordinate solve, long-only), then are scaled so sqrt(w' Sigma_t w) = 6%, with the remainder in cash. As p_t rises the sizing formula itself shifts risk toward low-vol assets (Treasuries, TIPS) and into cash, because the scenario covariance no longer credits diversification; the bound on drawdown is stated as a stress-covariance budget: under rho = 0.8 and 6% ex-ante vol, a 5-sigma 20-day loss is about 6% * sqrt(20/252) * 5 = 8.5%, well inside 20% even if the state lags. Execution: trade only on Monday, Wednesday and Friday (next trading day if a holiday), each session moving toward target with sells-to-cash filled first and total one-way turnover capped at 6.5% per session, so weekly turnover is at most 19.5% and there are 3 trading days per full week by rule. Novel element: a stress prior blended in by an eigenvalue-based state variable, rather than a trend or vol signal on individual assets, with the drawdown claim tied to how far AR leads price losses.

ideas.title: Droop-governed risk parity with a 4%-per-day ramp limit and a 10% spinning-reserve cash floor
ideas.sketch: The base target is inverse-volatility risk parity across all 10 ETFs (63-day volatility of daily close-to-close returns), and the controller acts on the drawdown of the strategy's own NAV from its trailing 252-day peak, which plays the role of the grid's frequency deviation. Target gross exposure follows a droop law with a deadband, E_t = clip(0.90 - 8*(DD_t - 0.04), 0.25, 0.90): there is no action inside a 4% drawdown, each further 1% of drawdown removes 8% of exposure, and the 0.25 floor is reached at about 12% DD, which leaves roughly 8 points of headroom to the 20% limit. The permanent 10% cash is the spinning reserve; it makes re-risking after a V-shaped recovery (as in 2020) possible without selling anything. Execution is ramp-limited: each trading day the portfolio moves toward target along the straight-line gap vector, scaled so one-way turnover sum|dw|/2 is at most 4%. Five days times 4% bounds weekly turnover at 20% by construction, and because the volatility estimates change with every close, the gap is almost surely nonzero, so trades happen on every day. To make that guarantee hold by rule rather than by probability, any Monday, Wednesday or Friday whose computed trade is below 0.05% instead makes a 0.05% 'reserve test' transfer between cash and the most-underweight ETF. The transfer is fairly literal (droop is essentially a drawdown-keyed CPPI, which is not new), but the ramp cap is a genuine contribution: it makes the turnover and frequency gates the control law itself instead of clipping bolted on. The honest weakness is that a 64-point de-risk takes about 16 trading days, so a 2020-style fall of about 10% in three weeks is only partly absorbed. My estimate is a worst case of about 13-16% DD and net growth of about 4.5-5.5% a year, taking unlevered risk-parity returns less the reserve drag and less than 10 bp of cost.

ideas.title: N-1 contingency reserve: size exposure so losing the largest asset-class 'generator' cannot breach the drawdown limit, with asymmetric primary/secondary ramps
ideas.sketch: The ETFs are grouped into three 'generating units', Equity (US large, US small, developed ex-US, EM, REITs), Duration (7-10y Treasuries, TIPS, IG credit) and Real (gold, broad commodities), and each unit gets equal risk contribution at the cluster level (63-day covariance of cluster returns); within a cluster the weights are inverse volatility, halved for any ETF whose close is below its 200-day SMA. Each day the rule computes each cluster's contingency loss L_c, the 1st-percentile 10-day return over the trailing 1260 days, and a correlated-stress loss S_t = max_c(w_c*L_c) + 0.5*sum_{other c}(w_c*L_c), which transfers the grid's N-1 criterion (the largest unit trips while the others sag) to a correlated sell-off such as 2008 or 2022. Invested exposure is lambda_t = min(0.95, H_t/S_t), where H_t = 0.17 - DD_t is the remaining drawdown headroom (the 20% limit less a 3-point safety margin), so cash is exactly the reserve needed to survive the largest plausible contingency, never less than 5%. The primary response (cutting risk) is ramp-limited to 4% one-way per day, and the secondary response (AGC-like restoration of risk) to 2% per day. With five trading days, even the worst mix is at most 20% weekly turnover, and the slower upward ramp damps the whipsaw oscillations that a symmetric controller would produce. Trading on three or more days follows from the daily covariance, L_c and DD updates, backed by the same 0.05% reserve-test dither on Mon/Wed/Fri. The transfer is stronger than plain droop, because N-1 sizing gives an explicit, auditable worst-case argument addressed to correlated stress, and the diversification rubric is met by rule because no cluster carries more than a third of the risk. The main doubt is that L_c from a 5-year window can understate a new regime (for example, 2022 bond losses after 2017-2021 calm), which the 3-point margin only partly covers; my net growth estimate is about 4-5.5% a year.

ideas.title: Effective-bets throttle with a daily turnover budget
ideas.sketch: Each close, build the 10x10 correlation matrix of daily log returns over a 63-day and a 21-day window, take its eigenvalues (they sum to 10), and compute the entropy effective number of bets N_eff = exp(-sum p_i ln p_i) with p_i = lambda_i/10, so N_eff runs from 1 (one factor) to 10 (independent). Divide each window's N_eff by its own trailing 756-day median (expanding after a 126-day minimum; the ratio cancels small-sample bias, which is worst at 21 days) and set total exposure s = clip(min(ratio_63, ratio_21), 0.25, 1); the fast window cuts risk early, the slow one delays re-entry. Target weights are s times inverse-volatility (63-day) weights, each capped at 20% of the sleeve with the excess redistributed pro rata; the remainder 1-s is cash, and s is the only use of correlation, so no return forecast is needed. Signals are computed at close t and traded at close t+1. Constraints hold by construction: every day one-way traded value is capped at 3.5% of NAV (5 x 3.5% = 17.5% per week, under 20% even if cash counts as a position), with priority to (i) sells that lower exposure, (ii) inverse-vol rebalancing, (iii) buys that raise exposure, scaled pro rata when the budget binds. There is no deadband, so any nonzero gap is traded on each of 5 days (at least 3 in every week). Rationale: the 20% drawdown bound is broken by correlated sell-offs (2008 risk-asset block, March 2020 liquidation, 2022 stock-bond correlation turning positive), each of which collapses N_eff before or during the loss. Honest estimate: the unthrottled inverse-vol book has about 6% volatility and roughly -16% in 2022, and the throttle should bring that to about -10% to -14%; the 17.5% weekly speed limit is the main residual risk in a one-week crash. Expected net growth is about 4-5% per year, from harvesting equity, credit, term, inflation and commodity premia at low risk, with cost drag under 0.3% per year at 3 bp per unit traded.

ideas.title: Down-day correlation gap ladder on Mon/Wed/Fri
ideas.sketch: The signal is the loss of diversification precisely on down days, following the known asymmetry that correlations rise when markets fall. Let m_t be the equal-weight mean of the 10 daily returns; over the trailing 126 days split days into down (m<0) and up (m>=0), and compute the average pairwise correlation of the 10 assets on each subset, rho_D and rho_U (about 55-70 observations each, standard error near 0.13, which is why 126 rather than 63 days). Set exposure E = clip(1 - (rho_D - rho_U)/(1 - rho_U), 0.25, 1), the fraction of the diversification headroom above the benign-state correlation that is lost in stress: E = 1 when down-day and up-day structure match, and E falls toward the 0.25 floor as rho_D approaches 1. Target weights are E times inverse-volatility (63-day) weights capped at 20% per ETF (excess redistributed pro rata to uncapped names), with 1-E in cash. Trades occur only on the first, the ceil((n+1)/2)-th and the last trading day of each week (n trading days: Mon/Wed/Fri in a full week), each capped at 6% of NAV one-way, which gives at least 3 trade days and at most 18% weekly turnover by construction, while ordering trades as de-risking sells first, then rebalancing, then buys; signals use the previous close and execute at the next trade-day close. Only three parameters exist (126-day window, 0.25 floor, 6% clip) and each has a stated principle: statistical precision of the correlation estimate, a floor that keeps the book diversified and invested, and a 20% budget divided over three days. The signal is meant to fire in equity-bond regimes such as 2022 (down-day correlation between stocks, bonds and credit jumps while up-day correlation stays low) and in 2008 and 2020; it lags a one-week crash, so the worst case is estimated at -11% to -15% for a book with about 6% base volatility, not proven below 20%.

ideas.title: Grossman-Zhou cushion Kelly on a 3-bucket risk-parity core, executed by daily largest-gap pair trades
ideas.sketch: Risky core: three macro buckets (Growth = US LC, US SC, Dev ex-US, EM, REITs; Nominal = Treasuries 7-10y, IG credit; Real = TIPS, gold, commodities), inverse-volatility within each bucket and equal risk contribution across buckets from a 120-day covariance of daily close returns, so no bucket exceeds 1/3 of core risk at any date. Total invested fraction follows the Grossman-Zhou growth-optimal rule under a drawdown constraint: f = min(1, (NAV - 0.82*HWM) / (NAV * L)), where L = 2.33 * sigma_core(60d) * sqrt(20) is a 1-in-100 twenty-day core loss floored at 6%; the remainder sits in uninvested cash, and the 2-point buffer below the 20% limit absorbs execution lag. Execution each trading day: compute target weights, sort per-ETF gaps, fill gaps that reduce total exposure first, then trade the largest overweight/underweight pairs until one-way turnover hits 4%, and if every gap is below 0.1% still trade the largest gap, so every trading day has a trade and weekly turnover is at most 5*4% = 20% by construction. The return mechanism is the diversified risk premia of three low-correlated buckets plus the rebalancing (diversification) return of about 0.5*(sum w_i*sigma_i^2 - sigma_p^2), with exposure mechanically cut as the cushion shrinks; in a 2008 or 2022 path, a 15% core loss over 20 days removes most of the cushion and the 4%/day de-risking lane reaches cash in at most 25 days, which should keep maximum drawdown near 18%.

ideas.title: Crisis-correlation risk parity: ERC on a stress-day covariance with per-asset trend gates and five weekday tranches
ideas.sketch: Estimate covariance only from stress days, defined as the 100 worst equal-weight 10-ETF daily returns in the trailing 500 days, and shrink it 50/50 toward the full-sample 500-day covariance; then solve equal risk contribution across all 10 ETFs on that matrix, so diversification is judged by how assets co-move in sell-offs. When stock-bond correlation turns positive, as in 2022, the stress matrix sees it within weeks and moves budget from Treasuries and IG toward gold, TIPS, commodities and cash, instead of trusting the 2000-2020 bond hedge. Per-asset trend gate: an ETF whose close is below its 200-day simple moving average has its ERC weight halved, and the freed weight goes to cash rather than to other assets, so no class inherits another's risk. The whole book is then scaled so that stress-covariance volatility equals 7% per year, with total weight capped at 100%. Capital is split into five weekday sleeves of 20% each; each sleeve rebalances fully to the current target on its own weekday, with its own turnover clipped proportionally at 20% of the sleeve, which gives trades on every trading day, at most 4% portfolio turnover per day and at most 20% per week, and a 5-day staggered response that averages out signal noise instead of fighting it.
